mainEntity.name: What happens if you leave a missing tooth untreated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Over time, the teeth next to the gap may gradually shift, the opposing tooth may begin to over-erupt, and the jawbone in the area may slowly lose volume. These changes develop gradually and vary between individuals, but they can affect bite alignment, chewing function, and oral hygiene.

mainEntity.name: Does bone shrink after losing a tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. When a tooth is lost, the jawbone in that area no longer receives the stimulation it needs to maintain its density. Over time, the bone can gradually reduce in volume through a natural process called resorption. The rate and extent of bone loss vary between individuals.

mainEntity.name: Can a missing tooth affect your face shape?

acceptedAnswer.text: A single missing tooth is unlikely to cause noticeable facial changes. However, when multiple teeth are missing over a prolonged period, the gradual bone loss can subtly alter the contours of the lower face, particularly around the cheeks and lips. These changes develop slowly over years.

mainEntity.name: Will neighbouring teeth move if a tooth is missing?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes. Without the lateral support of the missing tooth, the adjacent teeth may gradually drift or tilt towards the gap. The tooth in the opposing jaw may also begin to move into the space over time. The degree of movement depends on individual factors and the location of the missing tooth.

mainEntity.name: Is it always necessary to replace a missing tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Whether replacement is recommended depends on the location of the missing tooth, the impact on your bite and function, and your overall oral health. Your dentist can assess your specific situation and advise on whether replacement would be beneficial or whether monitoring is appropriate.

mainEntity.name: What are the options for replacing a missing tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: The main options include dental implants, dental bridges, and dentures. Each approach has different characteristics, and the most suitable choice depends on your oral health, the number and location of missing teeth, bone support, and your personal preferences. A dental assessment can help determine which option is right for you.

mainEntity.name: How long can you wait before replacing a missing tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no strict time limit, but the longer a gap remains, the more opportunity there is for surrounding teeth to shift and for bone to be lost. Having an early conversation with your dentist allows you to understand your options while more treatment choices may still be available.
